summary: Describes how TLS is used to secure QUIC. TLS provides the handshake that authenticates the endpoints and establishes keys, and QUIC uses those keys to protect its packets.

plainLanguage.summary: QUIC is an encrypted transport protocol that runs over UDP. This document explains how it borrows the TLS handshake to agree on keys, and then does its own packet encryption instead of using TLS records. TLS authenticates the two ends and sets up the keys; QUIC applies those keys to every packet it sends.

questions: how does quic key update work
subtitle: How TLS hands QUIC its keys, and how QUIC encrypts its own packets.

tldr.problem: QUIC needs authenticated, encrypted connections, but it does not carry TLS records over TCP, so the TLS handshake has to be fitted into QUIC's own packets.
tldr.mechanism: TLS handshake messages travel in QUIC CRYPTO frames, TLS hands QUIC secrets at each encryption level, and QUIC uses them for its own packet protection, header protection and key updates.
tldr.outcome: QUIC gets TLS 1.3 authentication and key agreement, including 0-RTT, while QUIC takes over the job of the TLS record layer.

today: RFC 9001 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the standard way to secure QUIC with TLS.

sections.title: Why QUIC Uses TLS
sections.content:
This document describes how QUIC is secured using TLS. TLS 1.3 provides critical latency improvements for connection establishment over previous versions: absent packet loss, most new connections can be established and secured within a single round trip, and on later connections between the same client and server the client can often send application data immediately, using a zero round-trip setup.

TLS gives two endpoints a way to establish a means of communication over an untrusted medium such as the Internet. It authenticates the peers and provides confidentiality and integrity protection for the messages they exchange. Internally it is a layered protocol: each content-layer message, such as a handshake message, an alert or application data, is carried as a series of typed TLS records, and each record is individually cryptographically protected before being sent over a reliable transport, typically TCP, which supplies sequencing and guaranteed delivery.

TLS provides two handshake modes of interest to QUIC. A full 1-RTT handshake lets the client send application data after one round trip. A 0-RTT handshake lets the client use information it learned previously about the server to send application data immediately, but that data can be replayed by an attacker, so 0-RTT is not suitable for carrying instructions that might cause unwanted effects if replayed.

The authenticated key exchange happens between a client and a server. The client initiates it and the server responds, and if it completes both ends agree on a secret that neither can control. TLS supports both pre-shared key (PSK) and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, and the two can be combined to give forward secrecy while still authenticating with a PSK.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS is the encryption layer that many web connections use. This document explains how QUIC, the transport protocol that runs over UDP, uses TLS. The two work together: TLS checks who the two ends are and agrees on secret keys, and QUIC uses those keys to encrypt each packet.

sections.title: How TLS and QUIC Split the Work
sections.content:
QUIC assumes responsibility for the confidentiality and integrity protection of packets. It uses keys derived from a TLS handshake, but instead of carrying TLS records over QUIC as it would over TCP, TLS handshake and alert messages travel directly over the QUIC transport. QUIC takes over the job of the TLS record layer.

Rather than a strict layering, the two protocols cooperate: QUIC uses the TLS handshake, and TLS uses the reliability, ordered delivery and record layer that QUIC provides. There are two main interactions. The TLS component sends and receives messages through the QUIC component, which offers TLS a reliable stream abstraction. And the TLS component gives the QUIC component a series of updates, including new packet protection keys to install and state changes such as handshake completion.

Applications do not send their data as TLS Application Data records. They send it as QUIC STREAM frames or other frame types, which are carried in QUIC packets. QUIC carries TLS handshake data in CRYPTO frames, each a contiguous block of handshake data identified by an offset and length. Those frames are packaged into QUIC packets and encrypted under the current encryption level. Because packets can be reordered on the wire, the QUIC packet type says which keys protected a given packet.

Data is protected at four encryption levels: Initial keys, early data (0-RTT) keys, Handshake keys and application data (1-RTT) keys. Application data can only appear in the early data and application data levels, while handshake and alert messages may appear at any level.

Several aspects of the TLS handshake differ when used with QUIC, and Section 8 of the RFC sets them out. QUIC requires authenticated protocol negotiation, so unless another mechanism is used, endpoints MUST use ALPN, and a failure to negotiate an application protocol closes the connection with a no_application_protocol alert, error code 0x0178. QUIC transport parameters travel in a TLS extension, quic_transport_parameters, which carries them in the ClientHello and the EncryptedExtensions. That gives those values integrity protection, and a peer that receives the handshake without the extension MUST close the connection with an error of type 0x016d. The TLS EndOfEarlyData message is not used with QUIC, and neither is the TLS 1.3 middlebox compatibility mode, because QUIC has no way to carry a change_cipher_spec record.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS normally wraps messages in records and sends them over TCP. QUIC does not use TLS records at all. Handshake and alert messages travel in QUIC frames, and QUIC encrypts whole packets itself. Data at four stages is protected differently: at the start of the connection, for early data, during the handshake, and for application data.

sections.title: Carrying TLS Messages in CRYPTO Frames
sections.content:
QUIC takes the unprotected content of TLS handshake records as the content of CRYPTO frames. TLS record protection is not used by QUIC: QUIC assembles CRYPTO frames into QUIC packets, which are protected using QUIC packet protection. QUIC CRYPTO frames only carry TLS handshake messages. TLS alerts are turned into QUIC CONNECTION_CLOSE error codes, and TLS application data and other content types cannot be carried by QUIC at any encryption level.

Each encryption level is associated with a different sequence of bytes, which is reliably transmitted to the peer in CRYPTO frames. The four levels correspond to three packet number spaces: Initial and Handshake encrypted packets use their own separate spaces, while 0-RTT and 1-RTT packets share the application data packet number space. Each chunk of data produced by TLS is tied to the keys TLS is currently using, so if QUIC has to retransmit that data it MUST use the same keys even if TLS has already moved to newer ones.

When an endpoint receives a packet with a CRYPTO frame, it sequences the data into the input flow using the offset and delivers new data to TLS in order. A packet from a previously installed encryption level MUST NOT contain data that extends past the end of the data already received in that flow, and a violation is a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION. A packet from a new encryption level is saved until TLS moves to receiving at that level; if TLS then provides keys for a higher level while data from the previous level is still unconsumed, that is also a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

The interface from QUIC to TLS has four primary functions: sending and receiving handshake messages, processing stored transport and application state from a resumed session and deciding whether it is valid to generate or accept 0-RTT data, rekeying in both directions, and updating handshake state. The handshake is complete when the TLS stack has both sent a Finished message and verified the peer's Finished message. The server MUST send a HANDSHAKE_DONE frame as soon as the handshake is complete, and the client considers the handshake confirmed when it receives that frame.

As a new encryption level becomes available, TLS provides QUIC with three items: a secret, an AEAD function, and a key derivation function. QUIC uses them to generate its packet protection and header protection keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Handshake messages travel in QUIC frames called CRYPTO frames, each holding a piece of the handshake data with its position in the stream. Each stage of the handshake has its own keys and its own packet number space. QUIC hands TLS the bytes it receives and asks TLS for the bytes to send next.

sections.title: 0-RTT, Sending Data Before the Handshake Ends
sections.content:
0-RTT lets a client send application data before the handshake is complete, by reusing negotiated parameters from a previous connection. The client remembers critical parameters and gives the server a TLS session ticket so that the server can recover the same information. That information includes the parameters that determine TLS state, the QUIC transport parameters, the chosen application protocol, and anything the application protocol needs. All information used to establish 0-RTT must come from the same connection. TLS 1.3 sets a limit of seven days between the original connection and any attempt to use 0-RTT.

QUIC does not use TLS early data. Instead, the max_early_data_size parameter is repurposed to hold the sentinel value 0xffffffff, indicating that the server is willing to accept QUIC 0-RTT data. To say that it does not accept 0-RTT, the server omits the early_data extension from the NewSessionTicket. The amount of data the client may send is controlled by the initial_max_data transport parameter supplied by the server. Servers MUST NOT send the extension with any other value, and a client that receives another value MUST treat it as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

A server accepts 0-RTT by sending an early_data extension in the EncryptedExtensions, and rejects it by leaving that extension out. A server always rejects 0-RTT if it sends a TLS HelloRetryRequest. When rejecting 0-RTT the server MUST NOT process any 0-RTT packets even if it could. When 0-RTT is rejected, the client SHOULD treat an acknowledgment for a 0-RTT packet as a connection error if it can detect the condition, and it MUST reset the state of all streams, including application state bound to those streams, because every connection characteristic it assumed may be wrong. A client MAY reattempt 0-RTT after a Retry or Version Negotiation packet, since those do not signify rejection.

Because 0-RTT has no replay protection, restrictions apply. The STREAM, RESET_STREAM, STOP_SENDING and CONNECTION_CLOSE frames carry application data and are potentially unsafe in 0-RTT, so a client MUST NOT use 0-RTT for application data unless the application in use specifically requests it. An application protocol that uses QUIC MUST include a profile that defines acceptable use of 0-RTT; otherwise 0-RTT can only carry QUIC frames that do not carry application data. A server MUST NOT use 0-RTT keys to protect packets, and once a client has installed 1-RTT keys it MUST NOT send any more 0-RTT packets.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client has talked to a server before, it can send application data in the very first flight, before the handshake finishes. This is called 0-RTT. The server must say whether it accepts that early data, and if it refuses, the client must start its streams again. Because an attacker can replay early data, the client may only send it when the application asks for it.

sections.title: Packet Protection: Keys and AEAD
sections.content:
QUIC protects packets with keys derived from the TLS handshake, using the AEAD algorithm negotiated by TLS. Version Negotiation packets have no cryptographic protection. Retry packets use AEAD_AES_128_GCM, which protects against accidental modification and limits the entities that can produce a valid Retry. Initial packets use AEAD_AES_128_GCM with keys derived from the Destination Connection ID of the client's first Initial packet. All other packets have strong protection for confidentiality and integrity.

Each encryption level has separate secret values for the two directions, and these traffic secrets are derived by TLS. The keys used for packet protection are computed from the TLS secrets with the KDF that TLS provides, using the HKDF-Expand-Label function from TLS 1.3 with the hash function from the negotiated cipher suite. The label quic key produces the AEAD key, quic iv derives the initialization vector, and quic hp produces the header protection key. Using distinct labels keeps QUIC keys separate from TLS keys.

Initial packets apply the same packet protection process but use a secret derived from the Destination Connection ID of the client's first Initial packet. HKDF-Extract with a fixed salt and that connection ID as the input keying material produces an intermediate pseudorandom key, from which a 32-byte secret is derived for the client with the label client in and for the server with the label server in. The hash function is SHA-256. Because the keys are trivial to determine, Initial packets are not considered to have confidentiality or integrity protection, and Retry packets use a fixed key and similarly lack it.

The AEAD is applied before header protection, and the unprotected packet header is part of the associated data. The nonce is formed by combining the packet protection IV with the packet number: the 62 bits of the reconstructed packet number are left-padded with zeros to the size of the IV, and the exclusive OR of the padded packet number and the IV is the nonce. The associated data is the contents of the QUIC header up to and including the unprotected packet number, and the plaintext is the payload of the QUIC packet.

Some AEAD functions have limits on how many packets can be encrypted under the same key and IV, and an endpoint MUST start a key update before exceeding any such limit. The limits set here keep overuse from giving an attacker a disproportionate advantage. For AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM the confidentiality limit is 2^23 encrypted packets; for AEAD_AES_128_CCM it is 2^21.5; for AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 the limit is greater than the number of possible packets, 2^62, and can be disregarded. The integrity limit, which applies to received packets that fail authentication, is 2^52 invalid packets for the AES GCM algorithms, 2^36 for AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 and 2^21.5 for AEAD_AES_128_CCM. An endpoint that reaches the integrity limit MUST immediately close the connection with a connection error of type AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC encrypts each packet with an algorithm that TLS agreed on. The keys come from the TLS secrets, but QUIC derives its own with its own labels so that they cannot be mixed up with TLS keys. The first packets of a connection use keys that anyone can compute from the connection identifier, so they are not really secret. Each algorithm has a limit on how many packets may be sent under one key, and the endpoint must switch keys before reaching it.

sections.title: Header Protection
sections.content:
Parts of a QUIC packet header, in particular the Packet Number field, are protected with a key derived separately from the packet protection key, the one produced with the quic hp label. It protects the least significant bits of the first byte plus the Packet Number field: the four least significant bits for packets with long headers, and the five least significant bits for packets with short headers. That covers the reserved bits and the Packet Number Length field, and for short headers the Key Phase bit as well. The same header protection key is used for the duration of the connection and does not change after a key update, which is what allows it to protect the key phase.

Header protection is applied after packet protection. The ciphertext of the packet is sampled and used as the input to an encryption algorithm, and the output is a 5-byte mask applied to the protected header fields with exclusive OR. The least significant bits of the first byte of the packet are masked by the least significant bits of the first mask byte, and the packet number is masked with the remaining bytes. Any unused mask bytes are unused.

The sample is taken starting from an offset of 4 bytes after the start of the Packet Number field, because a receiver does not yet know the length of that field, so the packet number is assumed to be 4 bytes long, its maximum encoded length. The same number of bytes is always sampled. An endpoint MUST discard packets that are too short to contain a complete sample, and packets are padded so that the combined length of the encoded packet number and the protected payload is at least 4 bytes longer than the sample required. The cipher suites defined in TLS 1.3, other than TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 for which no header protection scheme is defined here, have 16-byte expansions and 16-byte header protection samples. For a packet with a short header and an 8-byte connection ID protected with AEAD_AES_128_GCM, the sample takes bytes 13 to 28 inclusive.

For the AES algorithms the header protection function is AES-ECB over the 16-byte sample. For AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 it uses the raw ChaCha20 function with a 256-bit key: the first 4 bytes of the sample are the block counter and the remaining 12 bytes are the nonce, and the mask is produced by encrypting 5 zero bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte and the packet number of a QUIC packet are hidden with a separate key, so that a network observer cannot read them or tell how far along the connection is. The mask is computed from a sample of the encrypted packet. The receiver removes it before decrypting the packet, and any change to the header is caught by the decryption.

sections.title: Key Update
sections.content:
Once the handshake is confirmed, an endpoint MAY initiate a key update. The Key Phase bit says which packet protection keys protect a packet. It starts at 0 for the first set of 1-RTT packets and is toggled to signal each subsequent update, which lets a recipient detect a change in keying material without waiting for the first packet that triggered the change.

Initiating a key update results in both endpoints updating keys. This differs from TLS, where endpoints can update keys independently, and it replaces the TLS key update mechanism: endpoints MUST NOT send a TLS KeyUpdate message and MUST treat the receipt of one as a connection error of type 0x010a, which is equivalent to a fatal TLS alert of unexpected_message.

An endpoint initiates an update by creating a new write secret from the existing write secret with the KDF provided by TLS and the label quic ku, then toggling the Key Phase bit and using the updated key and IV for all subsequent packets. The header protection key is not updated. An endpoint MUST NOT initiate a key update before the handshake is confirmed, and MUST NOT initiate a subsequent update until it has received an acknowledgment for a packet sent with the current key phase, so that both peers have the new keys before another update can happen.

The peer detects an update when it processes a packet whose key phase differs from the value used for the last packet it sent, and then tries the next packet protection key and IV. If that works, the peer MUST update its send keys to the same phase in response, and it MUST update its sending keys before sending the acknowledgment that completes the update. An endpoint that sees a second update before it has sent any packet with updated keys containing an acknowledgment MAY treat it as a connection error of type KEY_UPDATE_ERROR, and the same error code applies when an acknowledgment arrives in a packet protected with old keys for packets that were sent with newer keys.

An endpoint MUST retain old keys until it has successfully unprotected a packet sent with the new keys, and SHOULD retain them for some time after that, because discarding them too early makes the peer see loss. Endpoints MUST be able to retain two sets of receive keys, the current and the next, and SHOULD wait three times the Probe Timeout before initiating a key update after an acknowledgment confirms the previous one.
sections.plainLanguage: A long connection needs fresh keys. QUIC has its own way to change them: a single bit in the packet header is flipped, and both ends then switch to the next set of keys. The TLS key update message is not used at all, because QUIC cannot carry it in the way TLS expects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the security considerations that apply to TLS also apply to the use of TLS in QUIC.

Use of TLS session tickets allows servers and possibly other entities to correlate connections made by the same client, so clients can choose not to enable resumption and SHOULD NOT reuse tickets.

0-RTT is exposed to replay attack. QUIC itself is not vulnerable to replay, except through the application protocol information it might carry: processing of QUIC frames is idempotent and cannot produce invalid connection states, and QUIC connections produce no effects that last beyond the life of the connection, except those of the application protocol it serves. TLS session tickets and address validation tokens carry QUIC configuration information between connections and MUST NOT be used to communicate application semantics; clients MUST treat them as opaque values. Managing the risk of replay with 0-RTT is the responsibility of the application protocol, which MUST describe how it uses 0-RTT and what measures protect against replay. Disabling 0-RTT entirely is the most effective defence against replay attack.

QUIC includes three defences against packet reflection attacks, in which a small ClientHello produces a large block of handshake messages and amplifies the attacker's traffic. The packet containing the ClientHello MUST be padded to a minimum size. A server responding to an unverified source address is forbidden to send more than three times as many bytes as it has received. And because acknowledgments of Handshake packets are authenticated, a blind attacker cannot forge them.

Initial packets are not protected with a secret key, so they are open to tampering by an attacker. QUIC provides protection against attackers that cannot read packets but does not attempt to provide additional protection against attacks where the attacker can observe and inject packets. Some tampering, such as modifying the TLS messages, is detectable, but some, such as modifying ACKs, is not. Data carried in Handshake packets can also be tampered with, but because that requires modifying TLS handshake messages, the handshake will fail.

Header protection uses a separate key from packet protection, and the analysis of the construction guarantees privacy of the protected header fields. Reusing the same key and ciphertext sample more than once risks compromising header protection, because protecting two different headers with the same key and sample reveals the exclusive OR of the protected fields. For the algorithms in this document the probability of two ciphertext samples being identical is one in 2^64. The header is transitively authenticated by packet protection, because the entire packet header is part of the authenticated additional data, so a protected field that was falsified or modified can only be detected once the packet protection is removed.

Timing side channels matter too. The whole process of removing header protection, recovering the packet number and removing packet protection MUST be applied together without timing side channels, and sending MUST be free of side channels that reveal the packet number or its encoded size. Generating new keys during packet processing could reveal that a key update has occurred, so an endpoint SHOULD generate and save the next set of receive packet protection keys ahead of time, or defer generation until it discards old keys so that only two sets of receive keys are kept at any point.
sections.plainLanguage: The first packets of a connection are not secret, so an attacker who can inject packets can try to confuse the handshake. QUIC limits how much a server can send before it has checked the client's address, so an attacker cannot use the server to amplify traffic. Early data can be replayed, so only the application protocol can decide whether that risk is acceptable.

data.title: Applying header protection
data.code:
mask = header_protection(hp_key, sample)

pn_length = (packet[0] & 0x03) + 1
if (packet[0] & 0x80) == 0x80:
   # Long header: 4 bits masked
   packet[0] ^= mask[0] & 0x0f
else:
   # Short header: 5 bits masked
   packet[0] ^= mask[0] & 0x1f

packet[pn_offset:pn_offset+pn_length] ^= mask[1:1+pn_length]

items.label: TLS alert
items.desc: The TLS AlertDescription value is added to 0x0100 to make a QUIC CRYPTO_ERROR code, sent in a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame of type 0x1c.

items.label: TLS KeyUpdate received
items.desc: Endpoints MUST treat the receipt of a TLS KeyUpdate message as a connection error of this type.

items.label: Missing extension
items.desc: The quic_transport_parameters extension was absent from the ClientHello or the EncryptedExtensions.

items.label: No application protocol
items.desc: ALPN negotiation failed, so the connection is closed.

items.label: KEY_UPDATE_ERROR
items.desc: Used to signal errors related to key updates.
